title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
text:
From 2×2 DiD to staggered TWFE
Why can two-way fixed effects (TWFE) put negative weights on treatment effects when the Goodman-Bacon weights are positive? The two decompositions average different things. Goodman-Bacon averages \(2\times2\) difference-in-differences (DiD) estimators. De Chaisemartin–D’Haultfœuille (dCDH) weights treatment effects in treated group-period cells. A DiD can subtract an effect even when the weight on that DiD is positive. (Goodman-Bacon 2021; de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020)
The note follows the path of the original notes. It starts from the familiar \(2\times2\) DiD and its regression. It then lets groups start treatment at different dates, and one example yields both decompositions. It ends by making the original conclusion precise and by stating what to do in practice.
Two questions stay separate throughout. Does a comparison subtract a control group’s changing treatment effect? Does TWFE equal the ATT we want to report? Removing the first problem need not resolve the second.

title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
text:
The 2×2 starting point
Start with two groups and two periods. One group is treated in period 2; the other stays untreated.

Let \(Y_{g,t}\) be the mean outcome of group \(g\) in period \(t\), and \(\Delta_{g,t}\) the average treatment effect (ATE) in that cell. The DiD is
\[
DID=(Y_{T,2}-Y_{T,1})-(Y_{C,2}-Y_{C,1}).
\tag{1}\]
Assume common trends: without treatment, both groups’ expected outcomes would change by the same amount. Assume also no anticipation: treatment has no effect before it starts. Then the expected DiD equals the expected effect in the one treated cell, \(\mathbb E[\Delta_{T,2}]\). This is the ATT for that cell, not an average effect for the whole population.
With sample means, the same number comes from an OLS regression on individual observations \(i\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_{i,g,t}={}&\beta_0+\beta_1\,\mathrm{Treat}_g+\beta_2\,\mathrm{Post}_t\\
&+\beta_3\,\mathrm{Treat}_g\times\mathrm{Post}_t+u_{i,g,t}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
\(\mathrm{Treat}_g\) marks the treated group and \(\mathrm{Post}_t\) marks period 2. The estimate of \(\beta_3\) equals the DiD in Equation 1.
Applied work has more units and more dates. Units such as states differ in their permanent levels, and each date can have its own common shock. The regression therefore replaces \(\mathrm{Treat}_g\) and \(\mathrm{Post}_t\) with group fixed effects \(\alpha_g\) and period fixed effects \(\lambda_t\):
\[
Y_{i,g,t}=\alpha_g+\lambda_t+\beta_{fe}D_{g,t}+u_{i,g,t}.
\tag{3}\]
\(D_{g,t}\) is the treatment indicator. This is the TWFE regression; \(\widehat\beta_{fe}\) denotes its OLS estimate. In the \(2\times2\) case it is the same regression as Equation 2, so \(\widehat\beta_{fe}\) equals the DiD. Unit or state fixed effects give the same treatment coefficient in the designs considered here.
Adding fixed effects is not the problem. The problem appears when groups start treatment at different dates. TWFE then combines several DiDs, and some of them use already-treated groups as controls.

title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
text:
A two-group, three-period example
Now let treatment start at different dates. Use Goodman-Bacon’s labels: \(k\) is the early timing group and \(\ell\) the late timing group. Here \(k=2\) and \(\ell=3\) are their treatment dates. The groups have equal sizes. Once treated, they remain treated.

A tilde marks an expectation that holds the treatment design fixed; the assumptions below define it. There are three treated effects: \(\widetilde\Delta_{k,2}\), \(\widetilde\Delta_{k,3}\), and \(\widetilde\Delta_{\ell,3}\). As in dCDH’s two-group illustration, call the two expected DiD comparisons \(DID_1\) and \(DID_2\).
Early versus late, periods 1–2. The late group is untreated at both dates, so this is a standard DiD. Under common trends,
\[
\begin{aligned}
DID_1
&=\mathbb E[(Y_{k,2}-Y_{k,1})-(Y_{\ell,2}-Y_{\ell,1})\mid\mathbf D]\\
&=\widetilde\Delta_{k,2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]
Late versus early, periods 2–3. The late group enters treatment. The early group is already treated at both dates:
\[
\begin{aligned}
DID_2
&=\mathbb E[(Y_{\ell,3}-Y_{\ell,2})-(Y_{k,3}-Y_{k,2})\mid\mathbf D]\\
&=\widetilde\Delta_{\ell,3}
  -(\widetilde\Delta_{k,3}-\widetilde\Delta_{k,2}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]
Both comparisons remove the common untreated trend. The second also subtracts the change in the early group’s treatment effect. If that effect grows, \(DID_2\) understates the late group’s effect. Common trends can hold exactly and this subtraction still occurs. (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020, sec. II.A; Goodman-Bacon 2021, equation (14c))
Comparisons that use already-treated units as controls are called forbidden comparisons (Borusyak et al. 2024). The July 2024 notes used this name for \(DID_2\). The name points to the subtracted effect change, not to a failure of common trends. Suppose the early effect does not change: it jumps once when treatment starts and then stays at that level. Then the extra term is zero and \(DID_2=\widetilde\Delta_{\ell,3}\). The outcome itself can keep trending; only the effect must stay fixed.

title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
text:
One coefficient, two decompositions
In this design, each DiD receives weight \(1/2\). Substituting the effects gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde\beta_{fe}
&=\tfrac12 DID_1+\tfrac12 DID_2\\
&=\tfrac12\widetilde\Delta_{k,2}
   +\tfrac12[\widetilde\Delta_{\ell,3}
               -(\widetilde\Delta_{k,3}-\widetilde\Delta_{k,2})]\\
&=\widetilde\Delta_{k,2}
   -\tfrac12\widetilde\Delta_{k,3}
   +\tfrac12\widetilde\Delta_{\ell,3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]
The first line is Goodman-Bacon’s decomposition. It averages DiDs, and both weights are positive. The last line is dCDH’s decomposition. It averages effects, and the early group’s period-3 effect receives weight \(-1/2\). This negative weight does not come from a negative weight on a DiD. It comes from inside \(DID_2\), the forbidden comparison, which subtracts that effect.

Software
bacondecomp (Stata, R)

Both decompositions are available in standard software. bacondecomp lists each comparison with its weight; the R version labels the type of \(DID_1\) “Earlier vs Later Treated” and the type of \(DID_2\) “Later vs Earlier Treated.” dCDH’s twowayfeweights reports the weight on each treated cell’s effect, together with the number and sum of negative weights. In this example, one of the three cell weights is negative, and the negative weights sum to \(-1/2\).
For the lab’s starting values, set the three effects to \((1,5,1)\) and untreated outcomes to zero. Then \(DID_1=1\) and \(DID_2=1-(5-1)=-3\). TWFE equals \(-1\), although all three effects are positive. The ATT across treated observations is \(7/3\).
Both groups can have the same effect pattern: 1 when treatment begins and 5 one period later. The negative coefficient needs neither a violation of common trends nor sampling noise. The numerical values illustrate the decomposition; the weights \(1/2\) apply to this particular design.

title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
text:
What the example assumes
The note narrows dCDH’s setting. Groups \(g\) are observed in periods \(t=1,\ldots,T\). Each group’s size, \(N_{g,t}\), stays constant over time. All units in a group have the same binary treatment, \(D_{g,t}\). Once treated, they remain treated. No group starts treatment in period 1; some groups may never start. The regression Equation 3 has no other covariates.
Let \(\mathbf D\) collect all treatment indicators. Following dCDH’s conditional notation, write
\[
\widetilde\Delta_{g,t}=\mathbb E[\Delta_{g,t}\mid\mathbf D],
\qquad
\widetilde\beta_{fe}=\mathbb E[\widehat\beta_{fe}\mid\mathbf D].
\tag{7}\]
The tilde means that we hold the treatment design fixed and average over outcome uncertainty. In a treated cell, every unit is treated, so its ATE is also its ATT. The lab has no sampling noise: its assigned \(\Delta_{g,t}\) equals \(\widetilde\Delta_{g,t}\).
For causal interpretation, assume common trends in outcomes without treatment, conditional on the treatment design, and no anticipation. The potential outcomes rule out effects of other units’ treatment. These assumptions allow treatment effects to differ across groups and to change after treatment. Common trends does not require observed treated outcomes to follow parallel paths. The appendix states the assumptions and connects the papers’ potential-outcome notation.
An exact identity for the sample coefficient and a statement about expected treatment effects are different results. Goodman-Bacon provides the first. dCDH provides the second under the outcome assumptions. Sampling error still affects an estimate from real data.

title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
section: From the example to a larger panel
text:
From the example to a larger panel
Goodman-Bacon groups units by treatment date. A \(2\times2\) DiD compares two timing groups across two time windows. A window may contain several periods. Its mean uses all those periods, rather than a selected pair of dates.
There are three types of comparisons: treated versus never treated; early versus late before late treatment; and late versus early after early treatment. The last type uses an already-treated group as the control; it is the forbidden comparison of the example. The comparison weights are positive and sum to one. They depend on timing and group sizes, not on outcome or effect values. The sample identity itself does not require common trends. (Goodman-Bacon 2021, Theorem 1)
dCDH instead writes the expected coefficient as
\[
\widetilde\beta_{fe}
=\sum_{(g,t):D_{g,t}=1}W_{g,t}\widetilde\Delta_{g,t},
\qquad
\sum_{(g,t):D_{g,t}=1}W_{g,t}=1.
\tag{8}\]
\(W_{g,t}\) follows the notation in dCDH’s introduction. It is the coefficient multiplying a cell’s effect. In Theorem 1, the authors write it as \((N_{g,t}/N_1)w_{g,t}\), where \(N_1\) counts treated observations. Thus \(W_{g,t}\) includes the cell’s share of treated observations; \(w_{g,t}\) does not. The lab displays \(W\), using this same convention.
A treated cell has a negative \(W_{g,t}\) when its treatment residual, \(\varepsilon_{g,t}\), is negative. This residual comes from regressing treatment on the fixed effects. Early groups are treated in many periods. Late periods contain many treated units. Together, these features can produce a negative residual in an early group’s later periods. Not every staggered design has negative weights. (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020, Theorem 1 and Proposition 1)
To connect the decompositions, expand each weighted DiD into its outcome means. Under the outcome assumptions, untreated trends cancel. The coefficients left on a treated cell’s effect sum to \(W_{g,t}\). A Goodman-Bacon weight applies to the whole comparison, rather than to any single cell. The appendix gives the formulas and their notation in each paper.

title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
section: When effects do not change over time
text:
When effects do not change over time

The July 2024 notes concluded that TWFE is free of this bias only when treatment effects do not change over time, and that such effects are uncommon in practice. The example confirms the mechanism: if each group’s effect stays constant after treatment, the forbidden comparison subtracts nothing. Two refinements make the conclusion precise.

First define the ATT
Use dCDH’s ATT, conditional on the treatment design:
\[
\widetilde\Delta^{TR}
=\sum_{(g,t):D_{g,t}=1}\frac{N_{g,t}}{N_1}\widetilde\Delta_{g,t},
\qquad
N_1=\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}D_{g,t}.
\tag{9}\]
It averages effects across treated observations, so a unit observed in two treated periods contributes twice. The lab uses this ATT. Goodman-Bacon’s parameter is instead VWATT, the variance-weighted average treatment effect on the treated. It averages the treatment group’s ATT in each DiD’s post window, using the regression’s positive comparison weights. The two need not agree. (Goodman-Bacon 2021, equation (15) and Section 3.1.1)


Constant effects remove the subtraction, not the weighting
If every treated effect is equal, TWFE, VWATT, and the ATT coincide, even if some cell weights are negative. Negative weights alone do not prove bias.
Now let effects differ across groups but stay constant over time. In Goodman-Bacon’s notation, these effects are \(ATT_k\) and \(ATT_\ell\):
\[
\widetilde\Delta_{k,2}=\widetilde\Delta_{k,3}=ATT_k,
\qquad \widetilde\Delta_{\ell,3}=ATT_\ell.
\]
Then \(DID_1=ATT_k\) and \(DID_2=ATT_\ell\). Yet
\[
\widetilde\beta_{fe}=\frac{ATT_k+ATT_\ell}{2},
\quad
\widetilde\Delta^{TR}=\frac{2ATT_k+ATT_\ell}{3}.
\tag{10}\]
TWFE gives each group half the weight, which here equals VWATT. The ATT gives the early group two-thirds because it has two treated periods. At \((ATT_k,ATT_\ell)=(1,3)\), TWFE is \(2\) and the ATT is \(5/3\). The gap comes from how the averages weight groups, not from any subtraction. The early group’s cell weights, \(1\) and \(-1/2\), multiply the same effect and combine to \(1/2\). That is how negative cell weights coexist with Goodman-Bacon’s positive weights.


“Only when” is too strong
Time-constant effects are sufficient to remove the subtraction, but not necessary for TWFE to equal the ATT. At \((1,2,6)\), the early effect grows and \(DID_2=6-(2-1)=5\) still subtracts a change. Yet TWFE and the ATT both equal \(3\). Changing one effect breaks this coincidence, so it does not justify TWFE when effects are unknown. The appendix gives the general condition.

title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
text:
When every group is treated
In period 3, neither group supplies an untreated observation. Common trends and no anticipation alone cannot identify both unrestricted period-3 effects. To see why, raise both untreated period-3 means by the same amount and lower both effects by that amount. Observed outcomes stay the same. TWFE also stays the same because its period-3 weights sum to zero. The ATT changes.
Keeping only the first DiD identifies the early group’s period-2 effect. It does not identify the full ATT. Effects in later periods require an untreated comparison or an additional restriction, such as constant effects. A regression does not establish that restriction. This calculation illustrates the assumptions’ limits; it is not an additional decomposition theorem.

title: Negative Weights in Staggered DiD
text:
What to do in practice
The July 2024 notes ended with practical advice. When treatment starts at different dates, do not rely on the TWFE coefficient alone. This applies to a single static coefficient and to an event study. The advice stands.

Diagnose the design. Goodman-Bacon’s decomposition shows how much weight goes to forbidden comparisons. dCDH’s weights show which cell effects receive negative weights, how many, and their sum. These diagnostics show how exposed TWFE is to changing effects. Neither proves bias in a particular application. Lab step 7 shows both summaries for a simulated panel.
Name the target. Decide which average answers the question: the ATT across treated observations, an average by timing group, or effects by time since treatment.
Avoid forbidden comparisons. Heterogeneity-robust estimators compare treated units only with units that are not yet treated or never treated. Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) estimate an ATT for each timing group and date, then aggregate. Borusyak et al. (2024) impute untreated outcomes using untreated observations. dCDH also propose an estimator that compares groups whose treatment changes with groups whose treatment does not (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020). Their later survey reviews these methods (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2023).
Check event studies too. Sun and Abraham (2021) show that a TWFE event-study coefficient for one period relative to treatment can mix in effects from other periods. Their estimator and those above avoid this.

No estimator removes the limit in the previous section. Effects in periods without an untreated comparison still require an additional restriction.

Use the interactive lab
The lab follows this note in eight steps. Step 0 is the \(2\times2\) case. Steps 1–4 load the two-group example with the four sets of effects in the table above. Three sliders set the effects, and the lab writes out Equation 6 with the current numbers. Steps 5–7 move to larger panels: where negative weights appear, what changes without a never-treated group, and what the diagnostics report. Each step links back to its section here. Free exploration loads any design and lets you edit effects, treatment dates, and group sizes.
Moving an effect leaves the treatment design, and therefore every weight, unchanged. Only the weighted effects change. In Panel View, \(\Delta\) is the assigned cell effect, \(W\) its dCDH weight, and \(W\Delta\) their product; a negative product need not mean a negative weight. Click a Goodman-Bacon comparison to see its four outcome means. Click a dCDH term to see how the comparisons add up to its cell weight.
The lab generates outcomes without sampling noise. Its effects are known because the reader sets them. They are not estimates recovered from observed data. In particular, the simulated linear untreated trend does not supply an assumption for identifying late effects in real data.

title: Appendix A — Technical details (optional)
text: The main note gives the argument. Open a section below for definitions, proofs, or the lab’s calculations. The notation comes from de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) and Goodman-Bacon (2021). Algebraic simplifications and numerical illustrations are identified as such.

title: Appendix A — Technical details (optional)
text:
A.1 Foundations

Potential outcomes and treatment effects
Follow dCDH’s Section I. \(N_{g,t}\) is the number of observations in group \(g\) and period \(t\). \(D_{g,t}\) is the group’s treatment status. Treatment is the same for all units in a cell, which the authors call a sharp design. The observed and potential cell means are \(Y_{g,t}\), \(Y_{g,t}(0)\), and \(Y_{g,t}(1)\). Define
\[
\Delta_{g,t}=Y_{g,t}(1)-Y_{g,t}(0),
\qquad
Y_{g,t}=Y_{g,t}(0)+D_{g,t}\Delta_{g,t}.
\tag{A.1}\]
dCDH calls \(\Delta_{g,t}\) the cell ATE. In a treated cell, all units receive treatment, so this also averages the effects on the treated units in that cell.
Goodman-Bacon’s Section 3 instead writes \(Y_{it}(k)\) for the potential outcome when treatment starts at \(k\), and \(Y_{it}(0)\) for the untreated outcome. Treatment has no effect before \(k\). For this note’s staggered design, dCDH’s treated outcome is understood along the unit’s actual treatment path. It does not mean switching treatment on for just one period. This correspondence allows effects to depend on time since treatment.


The assumptions used here
The note and lab restrict attention to a balanced panel with fixed group sizes. Every group is observed at every date. Treatment is binary, starts after period 1, and stays on. Some groups may remain untreated. There are no additional covariates. These restrictions are narrower than dCDH’s general setting.
Condition on the vector \(\mathbf D\) of cell treatments. For the causal calculations, assume that
\[
\mathbb E[Y_{g,t}(0)-Y_{g,t-1}(0)\mid\mathbf D]
\quad\text{is the same for all }g.
\tag{A.2}\]
This is common trends conditional on the treatment design. dCDH derives the corresponding restriction from independent groups, strong exogeneity, and common trends. We impose the conditional restriction directly. We also maintain no anticipation and no effects of other units’ treatment. The restriction concerns untreated outcomes, not changes in treatment effects.
Let \(\widehat\beta_{fe}\) be the treatment coefficient in the regression of \(Y_{i,g,t}\) on treatment and group and period fixed effects. dCDH writes \(\beta_{fe}=\mathbb E[\widehat\beta_{fe}]\). Its conditional notation is
\[
\widetilde\beta_{fe}=\mathbb E[\widehat\beta_{fe}\mid\mathbf D],
\qquad
\widetilde\Delta_{g,t}=\mathbb E[\Delta_{g,t}\mid\mathbf D].
\tag{A.3}\]


The ATT across treated observations
With \(N_1=\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}D_{g,t}\), dCDH defines
\[
\Delta^{TR}=\sum_{(g,t):D_{g,t}=1}\frac{N_{g,t}}{N_1}\Delta_{g,t},
\qquad
\widetilde\Delta^{TR}=\mathbb E[\Delta^{TR}\mid\mathbf D].
\tag{A.4}\]
The paper calls \(\delta^{TR}=\mathbb E[\Delta^{TR}]\) the ATT and uses \(\widetilde\Delta^{TR}\) for its conditional counterpart. The main note holds the treatment design fixed and therefore uses the latter. In a panel, \(N_1\) counts treated observations across dates. It is not the number of distinct people ever treated.

The coefficient equality applies to this note’s balanced panel without covariates. Units in a group have identical treatment paths, so using unit or group fixed effects gives the same treatment residual and treatment coefficient. The cell-effect correspondence holds with the treatment groups and design fixed. Goodman-Bacon defines \(ATT_k(\tau)\) within a timing group. We use \(t\) for this date throughout. dCDH makes the conditioning on \(\mathbf D\) explicit.
The papers also use \(N\) differently. dCDH counts observations across all dates; Goodman-Bacon counts distinct panel units. We avoid using \(N\) in the combined formulas below. Goodman-Bacon’s \(n_k\) is a share, not a unit count.

title: Appendix A — Technical details (optional)
text:
A.2 The two general decompositions

Goodman-Bacon’s sample identity
Theorem 1 and equation (10a) of Goodman-Bacon (2021) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\beta^{DD}
={}&\sum_{k\ne U}s_{kU}\widehat\beta^{2\times2}_{kU}\\
&+\sum_{k\ne U}\sum_{\ell>k}
\left[s^k_{k\ell}\widehat\beta^{2\times2,k}_{k\ell}
      +s^\ell_{k\ell}\widehat\beta^{2\times2,\ell}_{k\ell}\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.5}\]
The three terms correspond to treated versus never treated, early versus late, and late versus early. A timing group includes all units with the same treatment date. \(U\) contains never-treated units. The weights are positive for comparisons present in the design and sum to one. If \(U\) is absent, omit its terms. This identity does not require assumptions on potential outcomes.


dCDH’s treatment-effect weights
dCDH’s Section II.A defines \(\varepsilon_{g,t}\) as the residual from regressing treatment on group and period fixed effects. With time-constant group sizes,
\[
\varepsilon_{g,t}
=D_{g,t}-D_{g,.}-D_{.,t}+D_{.,.}.
\tag{A.6}\]
Here \(D_{g,.}\) averages treatment over a group’s periods. \(D_{.,t}\) averages across units at a date. \(D_{.,.}\) is the overall mean. These are dCDH’s mean conventions. For a treated cell,
\[
\varepsilon_{g,t}<0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
D_{g,.}+D_{.,t}>1+D_{.,.}.
\tag{A.7}\]
The residual is orthogonal to the fixed effects, so
\[
\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}\varepsilon_{g,t}D_{g,t}
=\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}\varepsilon_{g,t}^{\,2}>0.
\tag{A.8}\]
Strict positivity requires treatment variation after removing the fixed effects. If everyone starts treatment at the same date, the period effects absorb treatment.
The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem gives the sample identity
\[
\widehat\beta_{fe}
=\frac{\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}\varepsilon_{g,t}Y_{g,t}}
       {\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}\varepsilon_{g,t}^{\,2}}.
\tag{A.9}\]
Under the conditional common-trends restriction, the expected untreated component contributes zero to the numerator. Therefore,
\[
\widetilde\beta_{fe}
=\sum_{(g,t):D_{g,t}=1}W_{g,t}\widetilde\Delta_{g,t},
\qquad
W_{g,t}=\frac{N_{g,t}\varepsilon_{g,t}}
                    {\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}\varepsilon_{g,t}^{\,2}}.
\tag{A.10}\]
In Theorem 1 the authors separate this weight into two factors:
\[
w_{g,t}
=\frac{\varepsilon_{g,t}}
{\sum_{(g,t):D_{g,t}=1}(N_{g,t}/N_1)\varepsilon_{g,t}},
\qquad
W_{g,t}=\frac{N_{g,t}}{N_1}w_{g,t}.
\tag{A.11}\]
Thus \(\sum_{D_{g,t}=1}W_{g,t}=1\). In general \(\sum_{D_{g,t}=1}w_{g,t}\) is not one. Both weights have the sign of \(\varepsilon_{g,t}\). The uppercase notation is from dCDH’s introductory equation (1); the product above follows from its Theorem 1.
The sample coefficient need not equal a weighted sum of expected effects in a realized dataset. The difference is the regression’s outcome noise. The lab sets that noise to zero.


When does TWFE equal the ATT?
Subtracting the two averages yields
\[
\widetilde\beta_{fe}-\widetilde\Delta^{TR}
=\sum_{(g,t):D_{g,t}=1}\frac{N_{g,t}}{N_1}
    (w_{g,t}-1)\widetilde\Delta_{g,t}.
\tag{A.12}\]
Because the weighted mean of \(w_{g,t}\) is one, we may replace \(\widetilde\Delta_{g,t}\) on the right by \(\widetilde\Delta_{g,t}-\widetilde\Delta^{TR}\). This expresses the difference as a weighted covariance. If it is zero for the fixed design, the two conditional averages agree.
In the two-group example of the main note, the difference is
\[
\widetilde\beta_{fe}-\widetilde\Delta^{TR}
=\frac{4\widetilde\Delta_{k,2}-5\widetilde\Delta_{k,3}
          +\widetilde\Delta_{\ell,3}}6.
\tag{A.13}\]
At \((1,2,6)\) the numerator is \(4-10+6=0\), so TWFE equals the ATT although the early effect grows. At \((1,1,3)\) it is \(2\), giving the gap \(1/3\) between TWFE \(2\) and ATT \(5/3\). Equality at one set of effects says nothing about another.
dCDH’s Assumption 7 imposes the corresponding zero-covariance condition in expectation; Corollary 2 then gives \(\beta_{fe}=\delta^{TR}\). This is a sufficient condition that allows effects to change over time.


Direct verification of the example
With rows \((k,\ell)\) and columns \((1,2,3)\),
\[
D=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\varepsilon=\frac16\begin{pmatrix}-1&2&-1\\1&-2&1\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{A.14}\]
For equal group sizes, the coefficients on the six observed means in Equation A.9 are \(3\varepsilon_{g,t}\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\beta_{fe}
={}&-\tfrac12Y_{k,1}+Y_{k,2}-\tfrac12Y_{k,3}
     +\tfrac12Y_{\ell,1}-Y_{\ell,2}+\tfrac12Y_{\ell,3}\\
={}&\tfrac12[(Y_{k,2}-Y_{k,1})-(Y_{\ell,2}-Y_{\ell,1})]\\
&+\tfrac12[(Y_{\ell,3}-Y_{\ell,2})-(Y_{k,3}-Y_{k,2})].
\end{aligned}
\]
After taking expectations and applying the outcome assumptions, only the three treated effects remain. The following table shows their coefficients from each weighted comparison.

Late versus early, weight \(1/2\)

Each cell is one-third of the treated observations. Therefore dCDH’s lowercase weights are \((3,-3/2,3/2)\), while the coefficients multiplying the effects are \((1,-1/2,1/2)\). Negative coefficients on untreated outcome means are part of ordinary differencing; they are not negative weights on treatment effects.

title: Appendix A — Technical details (optional)
section: A.3 Formulas used in the lab
text:
A.3 Formulas used in the lab

Timing groups and time windows
Pool groups sharing a treatment date, using their unit counts to average outcomes. Follow Goodman-Bacon: \(k<\ell\) are two treatment dates, and \(n_k,n_\ell\) are their shares of panel units. For a timing group that is a single lab group, \(n_k=N_{k,t}/\sum_gN_{g,t}\) at any date.
The time windows in equations (10b)–(10d) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{PRE}(k)&=\{1,\ldots,k-1\},\\
\mathrm{MID}(k,\ell)&=\{k,\ldots,\ell-1\},\\
\mathrm{POST}(\ell)&=\{\ell,\ldots,T\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.15}\]
Early versus late compares PRE with MID. Late versus early compares MID with POST. For treated versus never treated, use the treated group’s own PRE and POST. Every window mean averages all dates in that window.


Comparison weights
Goodman-Bacon writes \(\bar D_k\) for the fraction of periods timing group \(k\) is treated. Its overall residual treatment variance is \(\widehat V^D\). In terms of dCDH’s cell counts and residuals,
\[
\bar D_k=\frac{T-k+1}{T},
\qquad
\widehat V^D
=\frac{\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}\varepsilon_{g,t}^{\,2}}
       {\sum_{g,t}N_{g,t}}.
\tag{A.16}\]
Canceling factors in Goodman-Bacon’s equations (10e)–(10g) gives
\[
s_{kU}=\frac{n_kn_U\bar D_k(1-\bar D_k)}{\widehat V^D},
\tag{A.17}\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
s^k_{k\ell}
&=\frac{n_kn_\ell(\bar D_k-\bar D_\ell)(1-\bar D_k)}{\widehat V^D},\\
s^\ell_{k\ell}
&=\frac{n_kn_\ell\bar D_\ell(\bar D_k-\bar D_\ell)}{\widehat V^D}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.18}\]
These are algebraic simplifications of the paper’s weights, with the same notation. They equal the values shown by the lab. The weights of all comparisons present sum to one when \(\widehat V^D>0\).


From a comparison to a cell effect
Within a DiD, a treatment group’s post mean has sign \(+\) and its pre mean has sign \(-\). The control group’s signs are reversed. Divide by the number of periods in each window when expanding a window mean. If a timing group pools several lab groups, also multiply each group’s mean by its share of that timing group’s units. Finally multiply by the comparison weight.
The inspection tables display the resulting coefficient on each treated cell’s effect. Adding that cell’s coefficients over all comparisons gives \(W_{g,t}\) in Equation A.10. These entries are coefficients from the expansion, rather than separate Goodman-Bacon weights. The two-group table gives a complete example.


Verification
The calculation engine was checked against a separate weighted least-squares regression of cell outcomes on treatment and fixed effects. Cell weights are \(N_{g,t}\). The checks cover unequal sizes, shared treatment dates, never-treated groups, changing effects, and individual effect edits.
Across 684 estimable designs, the largest difference from the independent regression was below \(2\times10^{-12}\). The checks also verified both decompositions and each cell’s coefficient summed over comparisons. A further 24 designs with no residual treatment variation were correctly reported as unidentified.
In lab step 1, the note’s two-group example, the lab gives TWFE \(-1\), ATT \(7/3\), comparison weights \((1/2,1/2)\), and cell weights \(W=(1,-1/2,1/2)\). These checks concern the implementation. They do not test common trends in any application.

Goodman-Bacon’s \(\beta^{DD}\) in equation (15) is a probability limit. dCDH’s \(\widetilde\beta_{fe}\) is a conditional expectation. The note uses the latter for its finite-design calculations. It does not equate a finite-sample conditional expectation with an asymptotic limit. Both papers explain the same subtraction of changing effects in already-treated controls.
The lab reports the count of negative \(W_{g,t}\) and their sum. In the small example, one of three weights is negative and the negative weights sum to \(-1/2\). Neither number alone establishes a violation of common trends or gives the size of the treatment effects.
The term forbidden comparison, for a DiD that uses already-treated units as controls, comes from Borusyak et al. (2024).
The core argument uses the two papers above. The practical section of the main note points to the following estimators and survey. They introduce no additional notation into this note:

Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods.
Sun and Abraham (2021), Estimating Dynamic Treatment Effects in Event Studies with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.
Borusyak et al. (2024), Revisiting Event-Study Designs: Robust and Efficient Estimation.
de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2023), Two-Way Fixed Effects and Differences-in-Differences with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects: A Survey.
